title: ITD 145 Final Exam Review
description: Built from the final exam study guide: descriptive statistics, distributions, inferential statistics, outliers, NumPy, pandas, cleaning, reshaping, linear regression and plotting.

questions.question: A hospital wants the average wait time across all 12,000 of its yearly emergency visits, so it times 300 randomly chosen visits. The 300 visits are the ___.
options: sample
population
parameter
census
questions.explanation: The group you actually measure is the sample; the 12,000 visits are the population.

questions.question: In the same study, the true average wait time across all 12,000 visits is a ___.
options: statistic
parameter
quartile
sampling error
questions.explanation: A number describing a population is a parameter. A number computed from a sample is a statistic.

questions.question: Which pair of symbols correctly labels the sample mean and the population mean?
options: μ for the sample mean and x̄ for the population mean, since mu comes first
σ for the sample mean and μ for the population mean, which is the usual pairing
x̄ (x-bar) for the sample mean and μ (mu) for the population mean
x̄ for both, because the two means are calculated with the same formula
questions.explanation: x̄ is the sample statistic and μ is the population parameter. σ is the population standard deviation.

questions.question: A sample mean will always be exactly equal to the mean of the population it was drawn from.
questions.explanation: Different random samples give different means. That sample-to-sample difference is sampling error.

questions.question: A researcher doubles the size of a random sample. What is the most likely effect on the sample mean as an estimate of the population mean?
options: It is guaranteed to equal the population mean, because the sample is larger now
It becomes biased, because a larger sample is harder to select at random
It is unchanged, because sample size has no effect on how accurate it is
It is likely to land closer to the population mean, because sampling error shrinks
questions.explanation: Larger random samples reduce sampling error, but they cannot guarantee an exact match.

questions.question: The values in a data set are 3, 5, 7, 7 and 8. Which comparison of the mean and the median is correct?
options: the median (7) is greater than the mean (6)
the mean (6) is greater than the median (7)
the mean and the median are both equal to 7
the mean and the median are both equal to 6
questions.explanation: Mean = 30 / 5 = 6; median = 7. The small values pull the mean below the median.

questions.question: What is the median of the data set 4, 9, 12, 20?
questions.explanation: With an even count, average the two middle values: (9 + 12) / 2 = 10.5. The mean is 11.25.

questions.question: Which measure of central tendency is least affected by a few extreme values?
options: mean
range
median
maximum
questions.explanation: The median depends only on the middle of the sorted data, so a huge or tiny value barely moves it.

questions.question: A data set has a minimum of 5, Q1 = 14, a median of 30, Q3 = 38 and a maximum of 90. What is the interquartile range?
questions.explanation: IQR = Q3 − Q1 = 38 − 14 = 24. The other numbers are range-style traps: 38 − 5 = 33, 30 − 14 = 16, 90 − 5 = 85.

questions.question: The second quartile (Q2) of a data set is the same as the ___.
options: median
mean
mode
IQR
questions.explanation: Q1, Q2 and Q3 mark the 25th, 50th and 75th percentiles; Q2 is the 50th, the median.

questions.question: A data set has a variance of 49. What is its standard deviation?
questions.explanation: The standard deviation is the square root of the variance, √49 = 7.

questions.question: The variance of a data set is expressed in the same units as the original data.
questions.explanation: Variance is in squared units (for example, dollars²). The standard deviation takes the square root to return to the original units.

questions.question: Two classes both average 75 on an exam. Class A has a standard deviation of 3 and class B has a standard deviation of 12. Which statement is true?
options: Class A's scores are more spread out around the mean than class B's scores
Class B must have the higher median, because its standard deviation is larger
Class B's scores are more spread out around the mean than class A's scores
The two classes have identical score distributions, because their means match
questions.explanation: A larger standard deviation means the values sit farther from the mean on average.

questions.question: In a histogram of retirement ages, most people retire near 65, but a few retire in their 40s. Which skew describes this distribution?
options: positive (right) skew
no skew at all
uniform skew
negative (left) skew
questions.explanation: The long tail points toward the low values on the left, which is negative skew. It pulls the mean below the median.

questions.question: Household income is strongly right-skewed. Which ordering of the three averages is typical?
options: mean > median > mode
mean < median < mode
median > mean > mode
mean = median = mode
questions.explanation: A few very large incomes drag the mean to the right of the median, and the mode sits lowest.

questions.question: In a perfectly symmetric distribution, the mean and the median are equal.
questions.explanation: Symmetry puts the center of balance (the mean) and the middle value (the median) at the same point.

questions.question: The spread measure calculated as Q3 minus Q1 is called the interquartile ___.
questions.explanation: The interquartile range (IQR) is the spread of the middle 50% of the data.

questions.question: Match each statistic to how it is calculated or what it describes.

pairs.right: The sum of the values divided by how many there are
The middle value once the data are sorted
The value that occurs most frequently
The average squared distance from the mean
The square root of the variance
The distance between the first and third quartiles

questions.explanation: Mean, median and mode describe the center; variance, standard deviation and IQR describe the spread.

questions.question: What is the MODE of this sample: [2, 3, 3, 5, 7, 7, 7, 9, 12, 12]?
questions.explanation: The mode is the value that occurs most often. 7 appears three times, more than any other value.

questions.question: What is the MEDIAN of this unsorted sample: [9, 1, 7, 3, 5]?
questions.explanation: Sort first: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9. The middle value is 5. Taking the middle of the list as given would give 7.

questions.question: What is the MEAN of this sample: [4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42]?
questions.explanation: The sum is 108 and there are 6 values, so the mean is 108 / 6 = 18. The median is 15.5.

questions.question: Which pair contains only measures of spread?
options: mean and standard deviation
median and interquartile range
mode and variance
standard deviation and interquartile range
questions.explanation: Mean, median and mode describe the center; standard deviation, variance, range and IQR describe how spread out the data are.

questions.question: A data set of home prices has a mean of $420,000 and a median of $350,000. What does this suggest?
options: The distribution is probably right-skewed, with a few very expensive homes
The distribution is probably left-skewed, with a few very cheap homes
The distribution is probably symmetric, with the prices evenly spread
The distribution is probably uniform, with each price equally likely
questions.explanation: The mean sits above the median when a few large values pull it up, which is positive (right) skew.

questions.question: In a right-skewed distribution, which measure of center sits farthest out toward the long tail?
options: the median
the mean
the mode
the midrange
questions.explanation: The mean is the most sensitive to extreme values, so it is dragged farthest toward the tail; the mode stays near the peak.

questions.question: A salary column includes one executive paid 100 times as much as everyone else. Which call best summarizes a typical salary?
options: df['salary'].mean()
df['salary'].max()
df['salary'].median()
df['salary'].sum()
questions.explanation: The mean would be dragged upward by the executive's pay; the median depends only on the middle of the sorted values.

questions.question: Two normal curves have the same mean. Curve A has a standard deviation of 2 and curve B has a standard deviation of 6. How do they compare?
options: Curve B is wider and has a higher peak than curve A
Curve B is narrower and has a higher peak than curve A
The curves have the same shape, since their means match
Curve B is wider and has a lower peak than curve A
questions.explanation: The total area stays 1, so spreading the values out lowers the peak.

questions.question: Maria scored 82 on an exam with a mean of 70 and a standard deviation of 6. Jon scored 75 on a different exam with a mean of 60 and a standard deviation of 10. Who did relatively better, compared with their own exam?
options: Maria, because her z-score of 2 is higher than Jon's z-score of 1.5
Jon, because his score is 15 points above his mean and Maria's is only 12 above hers
They did equally well, because both of the scores are above the mean of their exam
Maria, because 82 is a larger number than 75 and the exams can be compared directly
questions.explanation: Z-scores put different scales on a common footing: Maria (82 − 70) / 6 = 2.0; Jon (75 − 60) / 10 = 1.5.

questions.question: A random variable is best described as ___.
options: a variable whose value is chosen by the researcher before any data are collected
a variable whose numeric value is determined by the outcome of a random process
a variable that can take only the values 0 or 1 on each trial of an experiment
a variable whose value changes every time the program that uses it is run
questions.explanation: Examples: the number of heads in 10 flips, or the time until the next customer arrives.

questions.question: Which of these is a DISCRETE random variable?
options: the time a customer spends waiting in the checkout line
the weight of the groceries in a customer's shopping bag
the number of customers who enter a store in one hour
the temperature inside the store at noon on a given day
questions.explanation: Customers are counted in whole numbers. Time, weight and temperature can take any value in a range, so they are continuous.

questions.question: Which of these is a CONTINUOUS random variable?
options: the number of runners who finish a race within an hour
the number of laps a runner completes before stopping
the finishing place (1st, 2nd, 3rd...) of a particular runner
the time it takes a runner to finish a race
questions.explanation: Time can take any value in an interval (12.4 s, 12.43 s, ...). The others are counts or ranks.

questions.question: A random variable that can take any value within an interval, such as a height, is continuous.
questions.explanation: Continuous variables are measured; discrete variables are counted.

questions.question: Which statement describes a normal distribution?
options: It is symmetric and bell-shaped, with the mean, median and mode at the center
It is flat, with every value in the range equally likely to occur
It is skewed to the right, with the mean larger than the median
It counts the successes in a fixed number of yes-or-no trials
questions.explanation: The normal distribution is the continuous bell curve. Flat is uniform; success counts are binomial.

questions.question: Adult heights are normally distributed with a mean of 170 cm and a standard deviation of 10 cm. About what percentage of adults are between 150 cm and 190 cm tall?
options: about 68%
about 95%
about 99.7%
about 50%
questions.explanation: 150 and 190 are two standard deviations below and above the mean. Empirical rule: about 95% fall within two.

questions.question: Exam scores are normally distributed with a mean of 70 and a standard deviation of 8. About what share of students score between 62 and 78?
options: about 95%
about 50%
about 68%
about 99.7%
questions.explanation: 62 and 78 are exactly one standard deviation below and above the mean, so about 68% fall between them.

questions.question: Which situation is modeled by a binomial distribution?
options: the number of emails that arrive in a one-hour interval during the work day
the height of one adult selected at random from a large population
the number showing on a single roll of a fair six-sided die
the number of defective bulbs in a random batch of 25, where each bulb is defective or not
questions.explanation: Binomial: a fixed number of independent trials, each with two outcomes and the same chance of success.

questions.question: Which situation is modeled best by a Poisson distribution?
options: the number of customer calls received by a help desk in one hour
the number of heads that appear in 10 flips of a fair coin
the height of one student chosen at random from the campus
the face that shows on a single roll of a fair six-sided die
questions.explanation: Poisson counts how many events occur in a fixed interval of time or space.

questions.question: A random number generator returns a value between 0 and 1, and every value in that range is equally likely. The values follow a ___ distribution.
options: normal
uniform
binomial
Poisson
questions.explanation: A uniform distribution gives every value in its range the same likelihood, so its graph is flat.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a requirement for a binomial experiment?
options: the experiment has a fixed number of trials
each trial is independent of the others
each trial must have more than two possible outcomes
the chance of success is the same on every trial
questions.explanation: A binomial trial has exactly two outcomes, success or failure.

questions.question: A Poisson random variable is continuous.
questions.explanation: It counts events, so it takes whole-number values and is discrete.

questions.question: Match each distribution to the situation it describes.

pairs.right: Adult heights clustered symmetrically around an average
The number of successes in a fixed number of yes-or-no trials
The number of events occurring in a fixed interval of time
Every value in a range is equally likely to occur

questions.explanation: Normal and uniform are continuous; binomial and Poisson are discrete.

questions.question: A histogram is used to show ___.
options: the relationship between two numeric variables across many observations
the proportion that each category contributes to a whole
the median and the quartiles of a single numeric variable
the frequency distribution of a numeric variable grouped into bins
questions.explanation: A histogram counts how many values fall in each range of a numeric variable.

questions.question: Choosing very few bins for a histogram can hide features of the data, such as two separate peaks.
questions.explanation: Bin width changes how the shape looks. Too few bins smooth detail away; too many make the plot noisy.

questions.question: The bars of a histogram touch each other, but the bars of a bar chart are usually separated. Why?
options: A histogram's bins are consecutive ranges of a numeric scale, while bar-chart bars are separate categories
A histogram shows percentages, while a bar chart can show only raw counts
A histogram is always drawn horizontally, while a bar chart is drawn vertically
A histogram always has exactly ten bins, while a bar chart can have any number
questions.explanation: The touching bars signal a continuous scale with no gaps between the ranges.

questions.question: The number of coin flips needed to get the first head is a discrete random variable, even though there is no maximum number of flips.
questions.explanation: The possible values 1, 2, 3, ... can be counted one by one, so the variable is discrete even though the list never ends.

questions.question: If a random variable has infinitely many possible values, it must be a continuous random variable.
questions.explanation: Discrete means countable. A count with no upper limit has infinitely many values but is still discrete.

questions.question: Between any two possible values of a continuous random variable, there are more possible values.
questions.explanation: Between 170.1 cm and 170.2 cm lie 170.15 cm, 170.11 cm and so on without end, which is why exact values have probability zero.

questions.question: Which of these fully describes a random variable?
options: its mean, which summarizes the typical value of the variable
its probability distribution: the possible values and how likely each one is
its range, from the smallest to the largest possible value
its sample size, which is the number of times it was observed
questions.explanation: The mean and range are summaries. The distribution describes the whole behavior of the variable.

questions.question: A discrete random variable takes the values 0, 1 and 2 with probabilities 0.2, 0.5 and 0.3. What is its expected value?
questions.explanation: Expected value = Σ x·p = 0(0.2) + 1(0.5) + 2(0.3) = 1.1. It is the probability-weighted average, not necessarily a possible outcome.

questions.question: If you repeat a random experiment thousands of times, the average of the outcomes settles near the random variable's ___.
options: mode
range
sample size
expected value
questions.explanation: The expected value is the long-run mean, the probability-weighted average of the outcomes. For a fair die it is 3.5.

questions.question: Of 12 randomly chosen customers, each either clicks an ad or does not, with the same chance every time. The number who click follows which distribution?
options: binomial
Poisson
uniform
normal
questions.explanation: A fixed number of independent yes-or-no trials with the same probability of success is the binomial setting.

questions.question: The number of typos on a page is modeled with a Poisson distribution. Which statement about this variable is true?
options: It is continuous, because a page could have any number of typos at all
It is discrete, because it counts events and takes whole-number values
It is continuous, because the Poisson is just a type of normal distribution
It is neither discrete nor continuous, because the number of typos is random
questions.explanation: Counts are discrete. Poisson is not a variation of the normal curve; it models the number of events in a fixed interval.

questions.question: A lottery machine draws a number from 1 to 49, each equally likely. After 100,000 draws, a bar chart of how often each number came up would look ___.
options: bell-shaped
right-skewed
roughly flat
two-peaked
questions.explanation: Equal probabilities give equal long-run frequencies, a uniform distribution.

questions.question: In a normal, non-skewed distribution, the mean, median and mode are all equal.
questions.explanation: The symmetric bell shape puts all three at the center.

questions.question: A 95% confidence interval for a population mean is 48 to 56. Which interpretation is best?
options: 95% of all the individual values in the population lie between 48 and 56
We are 95% confident that the interval captures the true population mean
There is a 95% chance that the sample mean falls between 48 and 56
The true mean has a 95% chance of being exactly 52, the center of the interval
questions.explanation: The 95% describes the method: intervals built this way capture the true mean about 95% of the time.

questions.question: Which change makes a confidence interval NARROWER, all else being equal?
options: increasing the confidence level
increasing the standard deviation of the data
increasing the sample size
decreasing the sample size
questions.explanation: More data means a more precise estimate. A higher confidence level or more variability makes the interval wider.

questions.question: With the same data, moving from a 90% to a 99% confidence level makes the interval ___.
options: narrower
unchanged
shifted left
wider
questions.explanation: To be more confident of capturing the parameter, you have to accept a wider range.

questions.question: Why do researchers calculate a minimum sample size before collecting data?
options: To make sure the sample is large enough to estimate the parameter with acceptable precision
To guarantee that the sample mean will equal the population mean exactly
To avoid having to run any hypothesis test on the data once it is collected
To make sure that the data will follow a normal distribution when plotted
questions.explanation: A sample that is too small gives wide intervals and unreliable results.

questions.question: In hypothesis testing, the null hypothesis typically states that ___.
options: the effect is as large as the researcher expects it to be
there is no effect or no difference
the sample size is too small to draw any firm conclusion
the alternative hypothesis has already been proven to be true
questions.explanation: The null is the default claim that the test tries to find evidence against.

questions.question: A hypothesis test returns p = 0.03 at a significance level of α = 0.05. What is the correct decision?
options: Fail to reject the null hypothesis, because p is greater than zero
Accept the null hypothesis as proven, because p is a small number
Reject the null hypothesis, because p is less than α
Reject the alternative hypothesis, because p is below 0.05
questions.explanation: When p < α the result is statistically significant, so you reject the null.

questions.question: A hypothesis test returns p = 0.20 at a significance level of α = 0.05. What is the correct conclusion?
options: Reject the null hypothesis, because 0.20 is larger than 0.05
Accept the alternative hypothesis, because p is not equal to zero
Prove the null hypothesis true, because p is a long way from 0.05
Fail to reject the null hypothesis; the evidence is not strong enough
questions.explanation: p > α means the data are consistent with the null. That is not proof the null is true.

questions.question: Which statement best defines a p-value?
options: The probability of results at least this extreme if the null hypothesis were true
The probability that the null hypothesis is true, given the data collected
The probability that the alternative hypothesis is true, given the data collected
The proportion of the sample that falls inside the confidence interval
questions.explanation: A small p-value says the observed data would be surprising if the null were true.

questions.question: Rejecting a null hypothesis that is actually true is called a ___.
options: Type II error
Type I error
standard error
systematic error
questions.explanation: Type I = false positive. Its probability is the significance level α.

questions.question: Failing to reject a null hypothesis that is actually false is called a ___.
options: Type I error
standard error
Type II error
sampling error
questions.explanation: Type II = false negative: a real effect goes undetected.

questions.question: A drug trial concludes that a drug works, when in truth it has no effect. Which error occurred?
options: Type II error (a false negative)
Sampling error (the sample was too small)
No error, because the test result was significant
Type I error (a false positive)
questions.explanation: The null (no effect) was true but was rejected, so it is a Type I error.

questions.question: The significance level α is the probability of making a ___.
options: Type I error
Type II error
sampling error
rounding error
questions.explanation: Choosing α = 0.05 accepts a 5% chance of rejecting a true null.

questions.question: Which test is typically used to compare a sample mean to a target value when the population standard deviation is unknown and the sample is small?
options: z-test
t-test
F-test
Poisson test
questions.explanation: The t-test uses the sample's own standard deviation and the t distribution, which handles small samples.

questions.question: A z-test is appropriate when ___.
options: the data are categorical, with more than two labels for each value
the population standard deviation is unknown and the sample has 10 values
the population standard deviation is known and the sample is reasonably large
the variable that is being measured can only take whole-number values
questions.explanation: z-tests rely on a known σ (or a large n); otherwise the t-test is the safer choice.

questions.question: A value of 86 comes from a distribution with a mean of 70 and a standard deviation of 8. What is its z-score?
A student's z-score on a test is −1. What does that tell you?
options: Their score is one standard deviation below the mean
Their score is one point below the mean score of the class
Their score is one standard deviation above the mean score
Their score is one percent below the average of the class
questions.explanation: A z-score gives distance from the mean in standard deviations; the sign gives the direction.

questions.question: A z-score tells you how many standard deviations a value is from the mean.
questions.explanation: z = (value − mean) / standard deviation.

questions.question: A company tests whether a new training program changes employee productivity. Explain what a Type I error and a Type II error would mean in this situation, and say which one the significance level α controls.
questions.modelAnswer:
The null hypothesis is that the program has no effect on productivity.

A Type I error means rejecting a true null: concluding the program changes productivity when it really does nothing (a false positive). The significance level α is the probability of making this error, so choosing α = 0.05 accepts about a 5% risk of it.

A Type II error means failing to reject a false null: concluding there is no evidence of an effect when the program really does change productivity (a false negative).
rubric: Says the null hypothesis is 'no effect' (or no difference)
Describes a Type I error as rejecting a true null, or finding an effect that is not there
Describes a Type II error as failing to reject a false null, or missing a real effect
States that α is the probability of a Type I error
questions.explanation: Type I = false alarm, Type II = missed detection.

questions.question: Why do statisticians often like to have samples of at least about 30?
options: Because 30 is the legal minimum for publishing the results of a survey
Because a sample smaller than 30 cannot be used to calculate a standard deviation
Because with 30 values the sample mean becomes exactly equal to the population mean
Because the sample mean's behavior is then reasonably close to a normal curve
questions.explanation: This is the central-limit idea. About 30 is a rule of thumb, and skewed populations need more.

questions.question: What does it mean to call a result 'statistically significant'?
options: A result like this would be unlikely to happen by chance alone if the null hypothesis were true
The result is large enough to matter in practice for the people it affects
The result has been confirmed by a second, independent study of the same question
The null hypothesis has been proven false with complete certainty by the test
questions.explanation: Significance is about chance, set by α. It says nothing about the size or importance of the effect.

questions.question: A test is run at α = 0.05. Which of these results would NOT be called statistically significant?
questions.explanation: A result is significant only when p < α. 0.07 is above 0.05, so the null is not rejected.

questions.question: A researcher lowers the significance level from α = 0.05 to α = 0.01. What happens to the chance of a Type I error?
options: It increases, because fewer results can now be called statistically significant
It is unchanged, because α only affects how often a Type II error happens
It decreases, because the test now demands stronger evidence before rejecting the null
It drops to zero, because a stricter test can never reject a true null
questions.explanation: α is the Type I error rate. Lowering it makes false positives rarer, at the cost of more Type II errors.

questions.question: Why do analysts report a confidence interval alongside a sample mean, instead of the sample mean alone?
options: Because the interval replaces the sample mean once the sample is large enough
Because the interval proves that the null hypothesis has been rejected by the data
Because the interval lists every individual value that was found in the sample
Because the interval shows how precise the estimate is, which a single number cannot
questions.explanation: A mean of 52 could be 52 ± 1 or 52 ± 20. The interval's width communicates the uncertainty.

questions.question: A data set has Q1 = 12 and Q3 = 30. Using the 1.5 × IQR rule, which of these values is an outlier?
questions.explanation: IQR = 18, so the fences are 12 − 27 = −15 and 30 + 27 = 57. Only 60 lies outside them.

questions.question: By the common z-score rule, a value is flagged as an outlier when it lies more than ___ standard deviations from the mean.
questions.explanation: In a normal distribution 99.7% of the values are within 3 standard deviations, so anything beyond is unusual.

questions.question: A value has a z-score of −3.4. Under the z-score rule, what is it?
options: an ordinary value, because it is below the mean rather than above the mean
an outlier only if the value is also greater than the median of the data
invalid data that has to be deleted from the data set before analysis
an outlier, because it is more than 3 standard deviations below the mean
questions.explanation: The sign gives direction only. What matters is that |z| is larger than 3.

questions.question: In a box-whisker plot, the box spans from ___.
options: Q1 to Q3
the minimum to the maximum
the mean minus to the mean plus one SD
the 5th to the 95th percentile
questions.explanation: The box covers the middle 50% of the data, and the line inside it is the median.

questions.question: In a box-whisker plot, individual points drawn beyond the ends of the whiskers represent ___.
options: the mean and the median
potential outliers
the first and third quartiles
missing values
questions.explanation: Whiskers reach the farthest values within 1.5 × IQR of the box; anything past that is plotted as a dot.

questions.question: Which is a reasonable first step when you find an outlier in your data?
options: Delete it immediately, since outliers are always mistakes in the data
Replace it with the mean without checking anything else about the row
Investigate whether it is a data-entry error or a real but unusual observation
Ignore it, because outliers never change a statistic such as the mean
questions.explanation: Errors should be fixed, but real extreme values can carry important information.

questions.question: Which plot best shows how a company's monthly sales changed over two years?
options: pie chart
box-whisker plot
histogram
line plot
questions.explanation: A line plot shows a trend over an ordered sequence such as time.

questions.question: Which chart best shows what share of a budget goes to each of five spending categories?
options: pie chart
scatter plot
line plot
histogram
questions.explanation: A pie chart shows parts of a whole.

questions.question: Which plot is best for checking the shape of the distribution of exam scores?
options: pie chart
histogram
scatter plot
bar chart of student names
questions.explanation: A histogram bins the numeric scores so you can see skew, peaks and spread.

questions.question: Which plot best shows whether taller people tend to be heavier?
options: histogram
pie chart
scatter plot
line plot over time
questions.explanation: A scatter plot places each (height, weight) pair, revealing any trend or correlation.

questions.question: A bar chart is best used to ___.
options: show how one variable changes continuously over time
reveal the shape of the distribution of a numeric variable
display the quartiles and the outliers of a numeric variable
compare values across separate categories
questions.explanation: Each bar is one category (a department, a product); a histogram or box plot handles distributions.

questions.question: Match each plot to what it is best at showing.

pairs.right: The shape of a numeric distribution
The relationship between two numeric variables
A trend over time or an ordered sequence
The median, quartiles and outliers
A comparison across categories
The parts that make up a whole

questions.explanation: Choose the plot from the question you are asking of the data.

questions.question: Why is the IQR a more robust measure of spread than the range when one value in the data is extreme?
options: It uses only the middle half of the data, so a single extreme value barely changes it
It uses every value in the data equally, so an extreme value is averaged away
It is measured in squared units, which makes one extreme value matter less
It is recalculated after the most extreme value has been deleted by hand
questions.explanation: The range depends entirely on the two most extreme values. The IQR (Q3 − Q1) ignores the outer quarter on each side.

questions.question: A box-whisker plot has a long upper whisker, and its median line sits close to the bottom of the box. What does this suggest about the data?
options: The data are left-skewed, with the lower half more spread out than the upper half
The data are right-skewed, with the upper half more spread out than the lower half
The data are symmetric, with both halves spread out by the same amount
The data contain no values at all above the third quartile of the data
questions.explanation: A median near Q1 plus a long upper whisker means the top half of the values stretches much farther than the bottom half.

questions.explanation: The best choice depends on how much is missing and why.

options: find_duplicates() and drop_duplicates()
duplicated() and remove_duplicates()
duplicated() and drop_duplicates()
info() and drop_duplicates()
questions.explanation: duplicated() returns True/False for each row; drop_duplicates() returns the DataFrame without the repeats.

questions.question: What is the difference between unique(), nunique() and value_counts() on a column?
options: unique() counts the distinct values, nunique() lists them, and value_counts() adds them up
unique() counts how often each value occurs, nunique() lists them, and value_counts() sorts them
unique() lists the distinct values, nunique() sorts them, and value_counts() removes duplicates
unique() lists the distinct values, nunique() counts them, and value_counts() counts how often each one occurs
questions.explanation: For a column with values a, a, b: unique() gives [a, b], nunique() gives 2, value_counts() gives a 2, b 1.

questions.question: Which tasks are typical early steps when cleaning a DataFrame, after you have examined it?
options: Drop duplicate rows, drop rows and columns you do not need, and rename columns
Sort the index, convert every column into text, and drop every row that holds a zero
Plot each of the columns, fit a regression model, and then drop all of the outliers
Pivot the data, merge it with another table, and then reset the row index
questions.explanation: Examine first (info, describe, head), then remove what is not needed and tidy the names before dealing with types and missing values.

questions.question: A table has one row per product and one column per region. Which description fits it?
options: long format
wide format
stacked format
merged format
questions.explanation: Wide data spreads one variable (region) across several columns. Long data has one row per product-region pair.

questions.question: A survey table has one row per respondent, with separate columns Q1, Q2 and Q3 holding their answers. You need one row for each respondent-and-question pair so that you can plot every answer. What should you do?
options: Reshape the table from long to wide, for example with pivot() or unstack()
Drop the duplicate rows from the table, using drop_duplicates()
Reshape the table from wide to long, for example with melt() or stack()
Merge the table with itself, using pd.merge() on the respondent column
questions.explanation: One row per respondent with a column per question is wide format. Plotting and grouping are usually easier on long format.

questions.question: What is binning?
options: Converting each value into text so that the values can be sorted
Removing the values that fall outside the whiskers of a box plot
Splitting a DataFrame into a training set and a test set
Grouping continuous values into ranges, which can make trends easier to see
questions.explanation: Binning reduces detail on purpose. A histogram bins automatically, and pd.cut() bins a column explicitly.

questions.question: Which function groups a numeric column into ranges, such as age bands?
options: pd.cut()
pd.bin()
pd.split()
pd.band()
questions.explanation: pd.cut(df['age'], bins=[0, 18, 65, 100]) assigns each value to an interval.

questions.question: You change a column in a subset created by filtering df and get a SettingWithCopyWarning. What is the usual fix?
options: Ignore it, since the warning always means that the change was saved to the original
Create the subset with .copy(), or set values on the original with .loc
Convert every column of the DataFrame to a string before changing the subset
Delete the original DataFrame first so that only the subset remains
questions.explanation: pandas cannot tell whether your subset is a view or a copy. df2 = df[df['x'] > 1].copy() makes the intent explicit.

questions.question: You have January and February sales tables with identical columns, and you want one table containing every row from both. Which call does that?
options: pd.merge(jan, feb)
jan.join(feb)
pd.concat([jan, feb])
pd.pivot(jan, feb)
questions.explanation: concat stacks tables one under the other by default. merge and join add columns by matching on a key or the index.

questions.question: By default, pd.merge(df1, df2, on='id') keeps ___.
options: every row from both tables, with NaN filling the gaps (an outer join)
every row of df1 only, even when no match exists (a left join)
every row of df2 only, even when no match exists (a right join)
only the rows whose id appears in both tables (an inner join)
questions.explanation: Use how='left', 'right' or 'outer' to change that.

questions.question: What does emp.set_index('name') do?
options: Sorts the DataFrame alphabetically by the contents of the name column
Returns a DataFrame that uses the name column as its row index
Renames the index of the DataFrame so that it is called name
Removes the name column and discards the values that it held
questions.explanation: The name column moves out of the data and becomes the row labels.

questions.question: What does reset_index() do to a DataFrame whose index is currently the name column?
options: Deletes the index and the name values from the DataFrame permanently
Sorts the rows back into the original order of the source file
Moves the index back into a regular column and restores a 0, 1, 2... index
Resets every value in the DataFrame to NaN and starts over
questions.explanation: Add drop=True if you want to discard the old index instead of keeping it as a column.

questions.question: A DataFrame created without specifying an index gets which kind of index by default?
options: a MultiIndex built from the first two columns
an index made up of the column names
no index at all; rows are identified only by position
a RangeIndex of integers 0, 1, 2, ...
questions.explanation: The default RangeIndex counts the rows from 0.

questions.question: What is a MultiIndex?
options: An index with two or more levels, such as region and product
Two separate DataFrames that happen to share the same index
An index that contains repeated labels only
A list of the column names in the DataFrame
questions.explanation: set_index(['region', 'product']) builds one. Use unstack() to move a level into the columns.

questions.question: Which code returns the mean salary of each department?
options: emp.groupby('salary')['dept'].mean()
emp.groupby('dept')['salary'].mean()
emp.mean('dept')['salary']
emp['salary'].groupby().mean('dept')
questions.explanation: Group by the category, select the column to summarize, then aggregate.

questions.question:
The DataFrame emp has the columns dept, name, salary and years, with the default index 0 to 5:
0: Sales, Ana, 52000, 3
1: Sales, Ben, 61000, 7

5: HR, Fay, 55000, 6
Which department has the highest mean salary?
options: Sales
HR
IT
They are tied

questions.question: What does emp.groupby('dept')['salary'].agg(['min', 'max']) return?
options: one row per salary, with the department shown in two columns
a single row holding the overall minimum and maximum salary
one column per department, holding every salary for that department
one row per department, with the minimum and maximum salary as two columns
questions.explanation: agg() with a list applies each function to every group.

questions.question: What does emp.pivot_table(index='dept', values='salary', aggfunc='max') return?
options: the highest salary in each department, one row per department
the highest salary in the whole table, as a single number
the total salary of each department, one row per department
one row per employee, with the salary as the only column
questions.explanation: index sets the rows, values picks the column, and aggfunc says how to summarize each group.

questions.question: A DataFrame has two different rows with the same product and the same region. You call df.pivot(index='product', columns='region', values='sales'). What happens?
options: It adds the two sales values together, so that the cell holds their total
It raises an error, because pivot cannot handle a repeated product-and-region pair
It averages the two sales values, so that the cell holds their mean
It keeps the first row it finds and quietly discards the second row
questions.explanation: pivot only reshapes. pivot_table(..., aggfunc='sum') would combine the duplicates instead.

questions.question: What does unstack() do on a DataFrame that has a two-level row index?
options: Moves the column labels into a new row-index level, making the table longer
Removes the duplicated labels from the index of the rows
Moves the innermost row-index level into the columns, making the table wider
Splits the DataFrame into two separate DataFrames by level
questions.explanation: stack() does the opposite: it pushes columns down into the row index.

questions.question: Which operation turns the columns of a DataFrame into an innermost row-index level, making the table longer?
options: unstack()
pivot_table()
describe()
stack()
questions.explanation: stack() lengthens the table; unstack() and pivot_table() widen it.

questions.question: To split rows into groups by a column and then summarize each group, use the DataFrame method df.______('column').
questions.explanation: groupby() followed by an aggregate such as sum() or mean() is the pandas version of SQL's GROUP BY.

questions.question: Match each pandas call to what it does.

pairs.right: Makes the id column the row index
Moves the index back into a column and renumbers the rows
Pivots columns into the innermost row-index level
Pivots an index level out into the columns
Reshapes the data while aggregating repeated entries
Splits the rows into groups so each can be summarized

questions.explanation: Reshaping calls change the table's layout; groupby changes what is being summarized.

questions.question: Which code returns only the total units for each product in a DataFrame named orders?
options: orders.groupby('product')['units'].sum()
orders.groupby('product').sum('units')
orders['units'].groupby('product').sum()
orders.sum('product')['units']
questions.explanation: Group by the category, select the one column to total, then aggregate. Without selecting a column, sum() would add every numeric column.

questions.question: What does df['dept'].value_counts().plot(kind='bar') draw?
options: a histogram that bins the department names into equal-width ranges
a bar for each department, with the height showing how many rows it has
a line that follows the number of rows from the first to the last department
a pie slice for each department showing its share of the total salary
questions.explanation: value_counts() gives a count per category, and a bar plot is the right choice for categories.

questions.question: A DataFrame has one row per product and one column per region (North, South), holding sales figures. Explain what stack() and unstack() do, how they differ, and what each would do to this table. State whether the table is wide or long before and after.
questions.modelAnswer:
The table starts WIDE: each region is its own column.

stack() moves the column labels into the row index. For this table it turns the North and South columns into an inner index level, giving one row per (product, region) pair with a single sales column. The result is LONGER and narrower (long format).

unstack() does the reverse: it moves the inner row-index level back out into columns. Unstacking the stacked result gives back one row per product with a column for each region. The result is WIDER and shorter (wide format).

So stack = columns to rows (longer); unstack = index level to columns (wider).
rubric: Identifies the starting table as wide (regions spread across columns)
Says stack() moves columns into the row index, making the data longer
Says unstack() moves an index level into columns, making the data wider
Applies both operations to the product/region example correctly
questions.explanation: A common slip is reversing the directions: remember that stack makes the table taller.

questions.question: A correlation coefficient of −0.9 between hours of TV watched and exam score indicates ___.
options: a strong negative linear relationship
a weak negative linear relationship
a strong positive linear relationship
no linear relationship at all
questions.explanation: The sign gives the direction and the size (close to 1 in magnitude) gives the strength.

questions.question: A correlation coefficient close to 0 means ___.
options: the two variables are exactly equal to each other in every row
there is little or no linear relationship between the two variables
one variable causes the other variable to change by a small amount
the data contain mostly missing values in both of the columns
questions.explanation: Near 0 means a straight-line trend is absent; there could still be a curved relationship.

questions.question: A high correlation between two variables proves that one of them causes the other.
questions.explanation: Correlation measures association only. A third variable, or coincidence, may explain it.

questions.question: Which code returns a table of pairwise correlation coefficients for the numeric columns of df?
options: df.correl()
df.corrcoef()
df.corr()
df.relate()
questions.explanation: DataFrame.corr() returns the correlation matrix; corrcoef is a NumPy function, np.corrcoef.

questions.question: What does R², reported by a model's score() method, measure?
options: the average squared distance between the predictions and the actual values
the slope of the best-fit line drawn through the points of the data
the probability that each prediction made by the model is correct
the proportion of the variation in the target that the model explains
questions.explanation: R² runs from 0 (explains nothing) to 1 (explains everything) for a good fit.

questions.question: A model's R² on the test set is 0.82. Which interpretation is best?
options: About 82% of the variation in the target is explained by the model's features
The model's predictions are exactly correct about 82% of the time
The model's predictions are off by 82% of the actual value on average
82% of the rows in the test set were used to train the model
questions.explanation: R² is a share of variation explained, not an accuracy percentage.

questions.question: What does mean squared error (MSE) measure?
options: the average of the actual values minus the predicted values, unsquared
the average of the squared differences between the predicted and the actual values
the square root of the average difference between the model's features
the proportion of the rows that the model predicted exactly right
questions.explanation: Squaring stops positive and negative errors cancelling and punishes large misses. Lower is better.

questions.question: Model A has an MSE of 4 and model B has an MSE of 9, both on the same test data. Which statement is correct?
options: Model B is better, because a higher error means that the model has learned more
They are equally good, because MSE only reflects the size of the test set
Model A is better, because its predictions are closer to the actual values on average
Neither can be compared, because MSE is only comparable with R-squared values
questions.explanation: On the same data, the smaller MSE means smaller average error.

questions.question: In a model that predicts a car's resale price from its age and mileage, the dependent variable is ___.
options: age
mileage
age and mileage together
resale price
questions.explanation: The dependent (target) variable is what you predict. Age and mileage are the independent variables (features).

questions.question: Another name for the independent variables in a regression model is ___.
options: features
targets
labels
residuals
questions.explanation: Features are the inputs (X); the target or label is the output (y).

questions.question: Which equation describes a MULTIPLE linear regression model?
options: price = b0 + b1·sqft, which uses a single feature
price = b0 + b1·sqft + b2·bedrooms
bedrooms = b0 + b1·sqft, which uses a single feature
price = b0, a constant with no features at all
questions.explanation: Multiple regression has two or more independent variables; simple regression has exactly one.

questions.question: Which sequence describes the usual regression workflow in scikit-learn?
options: Fit the model on the whole data set, then split it into train and test sets to predict
Predict on the test set, then fit the model to the predictions that it made
Split into train and test sets, fit the model on the training set, then predict on the test set
Fit the model on the test set, then use the training set to predict
questions.explanation: The test set must stay unseen during fitting, or the score will look better than it really is.

questions.question: Why is a data set split into training and test sets?
options: To make the model train faster by reducing the data that it reads
To remove the outliers from the data before the model is fitted
To balance the number of rows that are held in each of the columns
To measure how well the model predicts data it was not fitted on
questions.explanation: Performance on the training data alone would overstate how well the model generalizes.

questions.question: train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25) is applied to 200 rows. How many rows go to the training set?
questions.explanation: 25% of 200 is 50 test rows, which leaves 150 for training.

questions.question: model.fit(df['sqft'], df['price']) raises an error. What is the likely fix?
options: Convert the price column into strings before the model is fitted
Pass the feature as a 2-D table, df[['sqft']], instead of the 1-D Series df['sqft']
Call model.predict() before calling model.fit() on the same data
Drop every row of df that contains a duplicate value in it
questions.explanation: scikit-learn expects X to be 2-D (rows × features), so use double brackets even for one feature.

questions.question: What does model.predict(X_test) return?
options: the R-squared score for the rows in X_test
the correlation between X_test and y_test
the model's predicted target values for the rows in X_test
the rows of X_test sorted by their predicted value
questions.explanation: predict() returns y-hat values. score(X_test, y_test) is what compares them with the truth.

questions.question: What is a heatmap of df.corr() used for?
options: to display the distribution of a single variable by grouping it into bins
to show how one variable changes over time by joining points with a line
to compare the totals of several categories using bars of equal width
to see at a glance which pairs of variables are strongly correlated, using color
questions.explanation: Each cell is one pair's correlation, colored by its strength and direction.

questions.question: Explain the difference between simple linear regression and multiple linear regression. Then give a realistic question that multiple regression could answer, and name its dependent variable and its independent variables.
questions.modelAnswer:
Simple linear regression predicts one dependent (target) variable from ONE independent variable (feature), fitting a line y = mx + b. Multiple linear regression predicts one dependent variable from TWO OR MORE independent variables.

Example: predicting a used car's resale price. The dependent variable is the resale price; the independent variables are the car's age, mileage and engine size.
rubric: Says simple regression uses one independent variable
Says multiple regression uses two or more independent variables
Gives a realistic example question
Names the dependent variable and at least two independent variables for the example
questions.explanation: Both predict a single target; they differ in how many features go in.

questions.question: Describe the steps you would follow to build and evaluate a linear regression model in Python, from a DataFrame to a score. For each step, name the function or method you would use.
questions.modelAnswer:
1. Choose the features X (for example df[['sqft', 'age']]) and the target y (df['price']).
2. Split the data with train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2) into training and test sets.
3. Create the model, LinearRegression(), and fit it on the training data with model.fit(X_train, y_train).
4. Predict with model.predict(X_test).
5. Evaluate on the test set with model.score(X_test, y_test) (R²) or mean_squared_error(y_test, predictions).
rubric: Separates the features (X) from the target (y)
Splits the data into training and test sets (train_test_split)
Fits the model on the training data only (fit)
Predicts on the test data (predict)
Evaluates with R² (score) or mean squared error
questions.explanation: The key idea is that the test data play no part in fitting.

questions.question: Which line displays the current Matplotlib figure?
options: plt.show()
plt.display()
plt.render()
plt.print()
questions.explanation: plot, hist, scatter and the rest only build the figure; show() draws it.

questions.question: What does plt.plot(x, y) draw by default?
options: a scatter of separate points with no line between them
a line connecting the (x, y) points in order
a histogram of the x values and the y values
a pie chart of the y values and their shares
questions.explanation: Use plt.scatter for unconnected points.

questions.question: Which code draws a histogram of the list scores using 8 bins?
options: plt.histogram(scores, bins=8)
plt.bar(scores, bins=8)
plt.hist(scores, bins=8)
plt.plot(scores, bins=8)
questions.explanation: The function is hist, and bins controls how many ranges the values are grouped into.

questions.question: Which code draws a scatter plot with height on the x-axis and weight on the y-axis?
options: plt.scatterplot(height, weight)
plt.points(height, weight)
plt.hist(height, weight)
plt.scatter(height, weight)
questions.explanation: plt.scatter takes the x values first, then the y values.

questions.question: Which sequence draws a scatter plot with a fitted line on top of it?
options: plt.scatter(x, y), then plt.plot(x, y_pred), then plt.show()
plt.line(x, y), then plt.scatter(x, y_pred), then plt.show()
plt.show(), then plt.scatter(x, y), then plt.plot(x, y_pred)
plt.hist(x, y), then plt.plot(x, y_pred), then plt.show()
questions.explanation: Both layers are added to the same figure before show() displays it.

questions.question: Which code draws a box-whisker plot of the list scores?
options: plt.box(scores)
plt.boxplot(scores)
plt.whisker(scores)
plt.hist(scores, box=True)
questions.explanation: matplotlib's function is boxplot.

questions.question: Which line labels the x-axis of the current plot as 'Height (in)'?
options: plt.label_x('Height (in)')
plt.axis('Height (in)')
plt.xlabel('Height (in)')
plt.title_x('Height (in)')
questions.explanation: xlabel and ylabel name the axes, and title names the whole plot.

questions.question: In sns.heatmap(df.corr(), annot=True), what does annot=True do?
options: annotates the color bar with the R-squared of the model
highlights only those cells that have values above 0.5
adds a title that names the DataFrame being plotted
writes each correlation value inside its cell
questions.explanation: Without annot, you see only colors and have to read the values from the color bar.
